definition.text: A planning and engineering approach, called WSUD, that builds the whole urban water cycle (stormwater, groundwater, wastewater and supply) into city design to limit environmental harm and improve amenity.

facts.text: WSUD is the term used in Australia and the Middle East; it resembles low-impact development in the United States and sustainable drainage systems in the United Kingdom.
It treats urban stormwater as a resource rather than a nuisance, a shift from conventional drainage that sent runoff quickly to streams.
Its principles include protecting urban creeks and wetlands, improving the quality of water leaving cities and maximizing reuse of stormwater, recycled water and greywater.
Common practices include bioretention systems, infiltration trenches, porous paving, sedimentation basins, constructed wetlands, swales and rainwater tanks.
The framework came out of Australia in the 1990s.
In Victoria, new residential developments must leave at least 20 percent of each site free of impervious surfaces.
Regulatory barriers and fragmented institutions across state and local government are major obstacles to its adoption.

title: Infiltration trench
article: Water-sensitive urban design#Infiltration trenches and systems

definition.text: A shallow trench filled with gravel or rock that holds stormwater underground and lets it seep slowly into the soil and groundwater.

facts.text: It is not mainly a treatment measure, but it can hold back some pollutants and sediment.
Sand filters work on the same principle and suit runoff from car parks and dense built-up areas.

definition.text: A basin that holds stormwater briefly and slows it so coarse and medium sediments settle out.

facts.text: It is often the first element of a treatment train, protecting later elements from being smothered by sediment.
Constructed wetlands often use a sedimentation basin as their inlet zone.

title: Floodplain restoration

definition.text: Returning all or part of a river's floodplain to its condition before levees were built and wetlands drained.

facts.text: Its goals include fewer floods, habitat for aquatic species, better water quality and more groundwater recharge.
Methods focus on reconnecting rivers to floodplains: setting back levees, removing dams or weirs, and restoring drained wetlands.
It is a nature-based solution that lowers flood risk by boosting the ecosystem's ability to slow and hold water.
Vegetation can cut wave energy during floods by about 70% in salt marshes and 65% in mangroves.
It works best for frequent, low to moderate floods and has limited benefit for extreme floods on its own.
Whether restoration increases coastal wetlands' carbon sequestration is debated, though their role in reducing flood risk is well supported.
Projects can stall when immediate flood defence and current land uses are valued above ecological benefits.
At Nijmegen, moving a dike 350 metres inland and digging a side channel lowered peak water levels by about 35 cm.

contested_note: Coastal wetlands are accepted as large carbon sinks, but whether restoration raises their sequestration rates is debated.
